clue.text: Rugby formation picking up a bone

indicators.note: the scrum picks up the letter a, holding it within its own letters

parts.note: a scrum is the formation of packed forwards in rugby

explanation.surface: A rugby scrum collapses and someone ends up with a broken bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The sacrum is the triangular bone at the base of the spine, between the hips.

clue.text: Somehow banks on the first person in Germany to provide food

indicators.note: the edges of the opening word act as banks either side of the on word, holding it between them

parts.note: its outer letters, the banks, are s and w
on can mean 'in addition', the same as and
the German for I, the first person pronoun, is ich

explanation.surface: Banks lend money to someone in Germany so that they can buy food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' works twice: it picks the outside letters of the opening word and has them flank 'on', a common stand-in for 'and' (plus).
explanation.definitionFit: A sandwich is a common snack of filling between slices of bread, a kind of food.

clue.text: React badly on Philistine's becoming artistic

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the first part sits above the next
something done badly is botched, so the letters of react are jumbled

parts.note: the setter, Philistine, refers to himself: Philistine's = I've (I have)

explanation.surface: A philistine, of all people, reacts badly by suddenly becoming artistic.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the setter's pseudonym means someone with no taste for art; here Philistine's stands for I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: Creative and artistic both describe someone with imagination and skill at making things.

clue.text: Foreign articles take advantage of court record's ultimate drama

parts.note: un is the French article 'a' and der the German article 'the'
to milk someone is to exploit them
to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: ultimate means the last letter of record's is taken

parts.note: its final letter is the d

explanation.surface: Some foreign outfit exploits the record of a court case to make a drama.
explanation.walkthrough: UN (French) and DER (German) are the foreign articles; Under Milk Wood is Dylan Thomas's radio play, the theme of this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Under Milk Wood is a 'play for voices' by Dylan Thomas, so a drama.

clue.text: Spend a penny gathering mud ants

indicators.note: gathering means holding the mud word inside the other word

parts.note: spend a penny is a British euphemism for urinating, here the vulgar piss
mire is deep mud

explanation.surface: Someone relieving themselves outdoors gathers mud and disturbs some ants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spend a penny' is British slang from coin-operated public toilets: to urinate.
explanation.definitionFit: Pismire is an old dialect word for an ant, named for the smell of an anthill.

clue.text: Half invoke All Saint's Day parody about truth after a few

indicators.note: half means taking the first three of the six letters of invoke

parts.note: its first half is inv
All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, I NOV

indicators.note: about means the parody word turns round and is read backwards

parts.note: a parody is a satire

explanation.surface: Someone half invokes a mock version of All Saints' Day, apparently after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: SATIRE read backwards gives ERITAS. The Latin phrase means 'in wine, truth'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin proverb says people speak honestly once drunk, so truth comes after a few drinks.

clue.text: Comedian running a country until recently

indicators.note: running here means in a state of flux, so comedian plus a is rearranged

explanation.surface: A comedian is running a country, a joke that was true until recently somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The Balkan state's name changed to North Macedonia in 2019, so it was the country's name until recently.

clue.text: Informer regularly talked to confuse

parts.note: a rat is someone who informs on others

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of talked, starting with the first

parts.note: its odd letters spell the last part

explanation.surface: An informer talks in order to confuse the investigators.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle someone is to unsettle or fluster them, throwing them off balance.

clue.text: From Caesar on Gaul: it's a wrap!

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words Caesar on Gaul

explanation.surface: Caesar's account of the Gallic wars, with a film-director's 'it's a wrap' at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's a wrap' sounds like a film set's sign-off, but wrap is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sarong is a length of cloth wrapped round the waist, a wraparound garment.

clue.text: Abundance of reflected light before first sign of dawn

indicators.note: reflected light is thrown back, so the light word is read backwards

parts.note: a neon is a kind of light

indicators.note: the first sign of dawn is its first letter

explanation.surface: Plenty of reflected light before the first glimmer of dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' is the idiom for a great deal; the 'of' is shared with the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'no end of' means a great quantity, so an abundance of something.

clue.text: Proponent of a doctor drinking vodka ends with separation

indicators.note: with separation means the two vodka letters do not stay side by side: one shifts to a new spot
drinking means the doctor takes the vodka letters inside

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the ends of vodka are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A doctor who drinks vodka ends up being separated from a spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With separation' is what stops the two ends of vodka sitting together inside the doctor: the first of them travels nearer the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An advocator is one who advocates, that is, a supporter who argues for a cause.

clue.text: Canine exchange to follow this legal framework?

definitions.text: Canine exchange to follow this legal framework?

parts.words: Canine exchange to follow this legal framework?
parts.note: a canine is a tooth, and 'a tooth for a tooth' follows this phrase in the Old Testament law of retaliation

explanation.walkthrough: Canine looks like it means a dog, but it is the tooth: the biblical rule continues 'a tooth for a tooth'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase states the Mosaic law of retribution, matching injury with equal injury.

clue.text: Invasive species weren't far out

indicators.note: out means the letters of weren't far are put out of order

explanation.surface: An invasive species turns out to have spread from somewhere not far away.
explanation.definitionFit: Water fern (Azolla) is a floating plant that spreads aggressively and is listed as invasive in Britain.

clue.text: One doubted if Bob is leading poet

indicators.note: is leading means the Bob word comes in front

parts.note: Bob Dylan, the singer-songwriter
the apostle Thomas doubted the Resurrection, hence 'doubting Thomas'

explanation.surface: A doubter wonders whether Bob is really the leading poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob Dylan took his stage name from the Welsh poet, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas was a Welsh writer of verse, author of 'Do not go gentle into that good night'.

clue.text: Mandarin orange centre shown in Sir Clive TV broadcast

indicators.note: shown in means the orange centre is placed inside the rearranged letters
broadcast means scattered, so Sir Clive TV is rearranged
the centre of orange is its middle two letters

parts.note: six letters, so its centre is two

explanation.surface: An orange is shown on Sir Clive Sinclair's TV, broadcast to the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mandarin orange' looks like one fruit, but Mandarin is the definition and orange gives AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandarin is a senior, powerful government official, especially in the British civil service.

clue.text: Zip up seaside town in play

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: zip, meaning nothing at all, is in British slang bugger all

explanation.surface: Someone zips up their coat in a seaside town during a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugger all' is a vulgar British phrase for nothing; Dylan Thomas built the town's name by writing it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Llareggub is the fictional Welsh fishing town in which Under Milk Wood is set.

clue.text: See 3
Wrong man needed to fashion graven image

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape anew, so the letters are rearranged, without those of man

explanation.surface: A wrong man is needed to make an idol, the graven image the commandments forbid.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of MAN out of GRAVEN IMAGE and rearrange GRVEIAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrieve someone is to wrong them, treating them unjustly and causing resentment.

clue.text: A dishwasher may be good for the opposition

definitions.text: A dishwasher may be good for the opposition

parts.words: A dishwasher may be good for the opposition
parts.note: a dishwasher spares effort; read differently, rescuing the Labour Party would suit its opponents

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is political: saving the Labour Party, which might help whoever opposes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour-saving describes a device that reduces work, as a dishwasher does in the kitchen.

clue.text: See 12
Nevertheless, tell the officer finally who did it!

parts.note: but and nevertheless both introduce a contrast

indicators.note: finally means each of tell, the and officer gives its last letter

explanation.surface: A detective-story climax: tell the officer who committed the crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The butler did it' is the cliché ending of a whodunnit.
explanation.definitionFit: In detective fiction the cliché culprit is the servant, so the guilty party is the household servant.

clue.text: Dressage de lycée?

parts.note: a lycée is a French secondary school, so a 'high school' of dressage

explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase literally means 'high school', which a lycée is; in English it names the most advanced classical riding.
explanation.definitionFit: Haute école is the most advanced form of classical dressage, with leaps and airs above the ground.

clue.text: Chrysler or Ford or a Team UK assembly

indicators.note: assembly means putting parts together, so these letters are put together in a new order

explanation.surface: Chrysler or Ford, or a British team's car assembly line.
explanation.definitionFit: Chrysler and Ford are both American car manufacturers, examples of the word.

clue.text: I don't buy this setter's issue of contention in 10

parts.note: the setter says my for something belonging to him
in an eye for an eye, the eye is what is being fought over

explanation.surface: The setter refuses to accept a point under dispute in another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is the clue AN EYE FOR AN EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My eye!' is an old exclamation of disbelief, meaning nonsense or I do not believe it.

clue.text: Mean Girls damned by harsh critics

indicators.note: damned means wrecked, so the letters of Mean Girls are rearranged

explanation.surface: The film Mean Girls is damned by harsh critics.
explanation.definitionFit: Maligners are people who speak spitefully and unfairly about others, hence harsh detractors.

clue.text: See 20
Like operating surgeons having clean place to sleep

parts.note: to scrub is to clean hard
a bed is where one sleeps

explanation.surface: Surgeons need a clean place to sleep between operations.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons scrub up before operating, so in theatre they are said to be scrubbed.

clue.text: Trade cycle report

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the cycle word is spoken aloud

parts.note: to pedal is to ride a bicycle

explanation.surface: A bike trade report, or a trade cycle report from an economist.
explanation.definitionFit: To peddle goods is to sell them, typically going from place to place.
